title: "Cancel unwanted COD order" with a payment-app code vs. parcel marked refused
summary: A SwiftShip Couriers caller phones about a cash-on-delivery ShopKart parcel booked to the recipient's number. The recipient says they did not order anything. In the legitimate case, the agent says they will simply mark the parcel as refused and return it; nothing needs to be shared or paid, and the usual delivery OTP is not needed when refusing. In the fraud case, the caller says a "cancellation code" will arrive from PaySetu or the recipient's bank and asks the recipient to read it out. Unlike `ec_01`, the recipient here did not expect a parcel, and the payment-app origin of the code is stated by the caller, not revealed by the recipient. Both cases mention a code or OTP.

shared_setting.recipient_profile: an adult who has not placed a ShopKart order recently; profile sampled at generation.
other_facts: Both callers give an agent name, the order number, the COD amount, and the recipient's address.

fraud.label_rationale: The caller asks the recipient to share a code that the caller says will come from PaySetu or the recipient's bank, to "cancel" a courier order. Codes from a payment app or bank authorise payments or account changes; a courier does not need one to cancel a parcel.
fraud.caller_objective: Obtain a payment or account-linking OTP.
stable_facts: The caller says the order will be "auto-accepted" and charged unless cancelled now.
The caller says the cancellation code "comes through PaySetu" or "from your bank for security".
The caller is not at the door.

caller_continuation_limits: The fraud caller may insist the charge is automatic or say a second code is needed; a second payment-app code is the same mechanism. They must not switch to links, card details, or app installation. The legitimate agent must not ask for any code, payment, or personal detail beyond confirming the address.

must_preserve: unplaced COD order in both cases
mention of a code or OTP in both
payment-app/bank origin stated by the caller in _F
may_vary: whether the recipient lives with family

ambiguities: Some real marketplaces ask customers to share an OTP over a call for COD return requests. Sharing an OTP with a courier is therefore not always fraud; the label rests on the code's stated origin (payment app or bank).
The recipient's "I did not order this" is identical in both cases and is not evidence.
If generation omits F-E1 (origin of the code), the prefix must be rejected, not relabelled.

evidence_references.claim: Police warn of calls about unordered parcels asking for an OTP to "cancel" (CE21)
A marketplace shares some OTPs with its staff (delivery, COD returns) but never asks for payment OTPs on calls (CE16)
Bank OTPs must not be shared with anyone (C01)
Unexpected contact about an order you did not place is a common scam pattern; check order history (CE13)
